passage:
Last year, in my second year of college, I was sure I had cracked it. I'm Harsh, and I had watched hours of videos about chart patterns on a video site. I drew lines on price graphs of small company shares in a trading app and called it my system.
The first week I made a little. Then I lost. My system said the price had to bounce, so I put in double to win it back. It dropped again. I doubled again. Each loss felt like proof I was close, like a puzzle I almost had.
My friends Disha and Mehak noticed I had stopped coming to the canteen. "Bhai, you look like you haven't slept," Disha said. Mehak was blunter: "You've lost your whole scholarship money, Harsh. That's not a system."
I was angry for a day. Then I showed my parents the screen, and we went to the college counsellor together.

qa.q: What did Harsh call the lines he drew on price graphs?
qa.a: He called it his system.

qa.q: Why did each loss feel to Harsh like proof he was close?
qa.a: Believing in his system made losses look like near misses in a puzzle he could solve, so doubling felt clever rather than risky.

qa.q: What was the turning point that stopped Harsh's losses from growing?
qa.a: Mehak naming the loss plainly, and Harsh then choosing to show his parents and see the counsellor, broke the cycle.

qa.q: How did Disha and Mehak experience Harsh's 'system' from the outside?
qa.a: They saw a friend vanish from the canteen and stop sleeping, which worried them enough to step in.

grounding: A young man believes his chart system will beat random price swings and keeps doubling after losses until friends step in.

passage:
Counsellor's notes, college wellness centre (Devika)
Wasim, 20, came in today after his roommate insisted. He talked fast about an online card game. He is sure he has a method: watch three rounds, then bet on the fourth. He showed me a notebook full of tallies. "I'm just unlucky this month. The method works. I only need to win back what I lost, then I'll stop."
He has lost his semester's hostel fees. Each time he lost, he says, he raised the stake "to fix it faster".
I didn't argue about probability. I asked how much he had slept this week, and how it felt to hide the notebook from his family. He went quiet, then said, "Tired."
Next steps: he agreed to a second session on Friday, to block the app with his roommate's help, and to think about telling his elder brother. I gave him details of a support group for gambling problems.

qa.q: What was Wasim's method in the card game?
qa.a: Watch three rounds, then bet on the fourth.

qa.q: Why does 'I only need to win back what I lost' feel reasonable to Wasim?
qa.a: His tallies make him feel in control, so losses look like temporary bad luck that his method will soon correct.

qa.q: Why was Devika's choice not to argue about probability a wise one?
qa.a: Asking about sleep and the hidden notebook reached how Wasim actually felt, which opened the door to real next steps instead of a debate.

qa.q: How might Wasim's roommate see the last few weeks?
qa.a: The roommate likely watched Wasim grow tired and secretive, and cared enough to push him to the wellness centre.

grounding: A counsellor notes a young man sure his betting method will win back his losses, raising the stakes after each one.

passage:
Tuesday, 1:40 am
Down again. Lost the evening on the over-by-over bets. But I KNOW the pattern: after two quiet overs, a boundary comes. I've watched a hundred matches. It came tonight too, just one over later than I bet.
So tomorrow I'll put in double. One good over and I'm back to zero, then I stop. Final time.
Nirmala saw my screen at dinner. She said, "Veerji, you said 'final time' on Sunday also." I laughed it off. She didn't laugh.
Writing it down, I notice I've said "one over later" about five times this week. If I were really in control, would I be awake at 1:40 writing this?
Maybe tomorrow I'll tell her how much it actually is.
Gurpreet

qa.a: After two quiet overs, a boundary comes.

qa.q: Why does Gurpreet plan to put in double tomorrow?
qa.a: Gurpreet feels confident he has read the game and only missed by an over, so doubling seems like skill fixing a near miss rather than a bigger gamble.

qa.q: What small choice in the diary could become Gurpreet's turning point?
qa.a: Telling Nirmala how much he has actually lost would bring the problem into the open, where someone he trusts can help him stop.

qa.q: How does Nirmala hear 'final time' after hearing it on Sunday too?
qa.a: To Nirmala it sounds like a promise that keeps moving, which is why she didn't laugh; she seems worried, not amused.

passage:
At the Shravan fair outside Kanhapur, a man with a loudspeaker spun a painted wheel: pick a number, pay twenty, win a hundred. Kunal, nineteen, had come to buy a sickle for his father. He lost on 4, then on 9.
"I'm reading it now," he told his sister Bhavna. "Watch how the man flicks his wrist. Soft flick, low numbers. Hard flick, high." He put forty on 2. The wheel stopped on 11.
"So, hard flick," Bhavna said.
"He changed it because he saw me watching. Next one I bet double and it all comes back."
By the time the lamps were lit, the sickle money was gone and Kunal was counting coins for the bus. On the dusty walk home, Bhavna carried the empty cloth bag. Kunal kept explaining the wrist, over and over, as if he had almost cracked it.

qa.q: What had Kunal come to the fair to buy?
qa.a: A sickle for his father.

qa.q: Why does Kunal feel he has almost cracked the wheel, even after losing the sickle money?
qa.a: Studying the man's wrist gives Kunal a feeling of skill, so each loss seems like a small reading mistake to fix with a bigger bet, not a sign that the wheel is random.

qa.q: At which moment could Kunal have made a better choice, and what would it be?
qa.a: After the first two losses, when he began "reading" the wrist; walking away then, or handing the sickle money to Bhavna to keep, would have saved it.

qa.q: What is the walk home like for Bhavna?
qa.a: Bhavna carries the empty bag and hears the same explanation again and again; she is probably worried about their father's money and tired of a brother who won't admit the wheel beat him.

grounding: It shows a young man who thinks he can read a spinning wheel, doubling his bets after losses until the money is gone.

passage: It was 1 a.m., the night before his final-semester exam, and Kamal was still on the betting app. He had a system: after every loss, double the next bet, because "a win has to come, and it'll cover everything." He had lost six in a row. His hands were cold. His exam notes lay unopened on the bed. His sister Mahima, home for the holidays, saw the light under his door and came in. She looked at the screen, then at his face. "Kamal. How much?" He told her. She didn't shout. She closed the laptop gently, sat beside him and said, "Tomorrow, after your exam, we talk to Papa, and we call a gambling helpline together. Tonight, you sleep." Kamal wanted to argue about his system. Instead he let her take the laptop to her room.

qa.q: How many losses in a row had Kamal had?
qa.a: Six in a row.

qa.q: Why did Kamal keep doubling his bets?
qa.a: He felt in control and sure his system would bring a win to cover everything, even as his hands went cold with fear.

qa.q: What did Mahima do, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She stayed calm, closed the laptop, took it away for the night, and planned to talk to Papa and call a gambling helpline together after the exam.

qa.q: What was it like for Mahima to see the screen?
qa.a: Mahima was probably frightened and worried for Kamal, but chose calm and care over shouting.

grounding: On the night before an exam, a young man doubles his bets believing his system will win it back, and his sister steps in that night.

passage: In the shared flat in Andheri, Tanvir's phone buzzed every few minutes with price alerts. He had started trading with his first salary, and he was sure he had a method: three green candles in a row meant buy, and a red one meant the market was "about to bounce." When a trade went wrong, he put in more to "average down." By March he had lost most of four months' savings. "I just need one good week," he told his flatmate Santosh at dinner. "I'm learning the patterns." Santosh put down his plate. "Tanvir, the price doesn't know your patterns. Every time you lose, you put in more. That's what worries me." Tanvir laughed, but his leg was jiggling under the table. Santosh slid a card across: the number of a certified financial counsellor his cousin had seen.

qa.q: What did Tanvir think three green candles meant?
qa.a: Buy.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir keep putting in more after losses?
qa.a: He feels confident he is learning the patterns and anxious to win the savings back, so putting in more feels like control.

qa.q: What does Santosh do that could help?
qa.a: He names his worry about Tanvir adding money after every loss and passes on a certified financial counsellor's number.

qa.q: How does Santosh seem to feel about Tanvir's trading?
qa.a: Santosh is worried, noticing the losses and the nervous jiggling leg under the laugh.

grounding: A young man believes his trading method can beat random price moves and keeps adding money after losses, while a flatmate voices concern.

passage: I'm Vishal, and last year, in my second year of college, I thought I'd cracked the online card game. I had a system: sit at the right table, fold a lot, bet big on certain hands. The first week I won a little, and it felt like proof. Then I started losing. Each time, I doubled the next bet, sure my system would win it back. My skill had to beat luck eventually. "Show me the app," he said quietly. I did. He didn't lecture. He sat with me while I called the helpline number on the college notice board, and the next morning walked me to the counsellor.

passage:
College counsellor's note, 9 February.
Saurabh, second-year commerce, came in today with his sister Sarita, who had asked for the appointment. Over three months he has been doing day-trading on his phone with money from his part-time job and a loan from a friend. He showed me a notebook of rules he calls his "system." He believes his chart reading gives him control, and that after each loss he must trade bigger to recover. His losses have grown each week.
He was defensive at first. When Sarita said she had heard him awake at 3 a.m. checking prices, he went quiet.
We agreed today: he will delete the app with Sarita present, and he will meet a financial counsellor from the helpline I gave him. I will see him again on Friday.

qa.q: Who asked for Saurabh's appointment with the counsellor?
qa.a: His sister Sarita.

qa.q: What does Saurabh's notebook of rules suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels in control and confident, believing his chart-reading system can beat what are really random price swings.

qa.q: What steps were agreed, and why are they helpful?
qa.a: Deleting the app with Sarita present and meeting a financial counsellor from the helpline, which remove the temptation and bring in expert support.

qa.q: How might Sarita have felt hearing Saurabh awake at 3 a.m.?
qa.a: Sarita was likely very worried about her brother, which is why she arranged the appointment and came with him.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young adult believing his trading system can beat randomness and trading bigger after losses.

She sat with me while I deleted the app, and she called a helpline for young people with gambling problems. I have an appointment tomorrow. I feel ashamed. But also like I can breathe.

Every evening after closing the phone repair shop in Kottayam town, Jomon stopped at the lottery stall by the bus stand.
He had a notebook now. Numbers that had won, numbers that were "due", and a column for what he'd spent. The column was getting long. When he lost, the system said buy double the next day.
"Two hundred yesterday, four hundred today," Abhinav read over his shoulder. "Machane, this is your rent."
"That's why I'm careful," Jomon said. "I study it. People who lose are the ones who pick randomly."
He handed over the notes. The stall-keeper gave him eight tickets. Jomon ran his thumb over them, calm for the first time all day.
Abhinav didn't laugh. He just said, "Come for tea first. Leave the notebook with me tonight."

qa.q: What did the system tell Jomon to do after a loss?
qa.a: When Jomon lost, the system said to buy double the next day.

qa.q: Why did Jomon feel calm holding the eight tickets?
qa.a: The notebook and system gave Jomon a comforting sense of control, as if studying numbers could make a random draw go his way.

qa.q: What could help Jomon step back from the notebook system?
qa.a: Talking it through with Abhinav and with a counsellor or a gambling support line, since the doubling now eats into rent money.

qa.q: How does Abhinav see Jomon's notebook?
qa.a: Abhinav sees it as a worrying sign, not a clever system, and gently offers tea and to keep the notebook for the night.

grounding: Shows a young adult who believes a numbers system can beat a lottery and doubles his spending after each loss.

Omar's desk in the Leeds flat was covered in printed tables: shots on target, home form, referee cards. He called it the model.
"Fourth loss in a row," Kaito said, looking at the betting site open on Omar's laptop.
"Variance," Omar said. "The model's right over time. I just stake bigger now to cover the last four."
"How much bigger?"
Omar didn't answer. He'd moved his grocery money into the account that morning, and it felt fine, because a system wasn't gambling. Gambling was for people who guessed.
The match kicked off. In the 88th minute, a shot deflected in off someone's knee. Omar stared at the screen.
"That's not in the model," he said quietly.
Kaito closed the laptop gently. "Let's go for a walk. When we're back, let's ring the uni's student support line together."

qa.q: What did Omar call the printed tables on his desk?
qa.a: Omar called them the model.

qa.q: Why did moving the grocery money feel fine to Omar?
qa.a: Omar felt confident and safe believing a system wasn't gambling, so risking more after four losses felt like skill, not chance.

qa.q: What could Omar do after the walk?
qa.a: Omar could ring the university's student support line with Kaito and talk honestly about the losses, instead of raising stakes to cover them.

passage: During the Puja holidays the hostel was nearly empty, and Yogesh spent most nights hunched over his phone in the common room. He had a notebook full of arrows and columns: his system for the colour-prediction game. "It's pattern reading," he told Ganga, who was warming milk on the pantry stove. "Red came four times, so I double on green. If I lose, I double again. Maths says I have to win eventually." "How much are you down?" she asked. He waved a hand. "That's temporary. I've been reading patterns for a month." By midnight he had borrowed from two friends online. When the screen showed red again, he didn't sleep. At breakfast Ganga sat beside him with two cups of chai. "I'm worried about you. Can we go and see the counsellor together today?" He stared at his notebook for a long time, then nodded.

qa.q: What did Yogesh do each time he lost?
qa.a: He doubled again, following his system.

qa.q: Why does Yogesh keep playing even as he loses?
